subject: ai
question: Can the exact figure 47.3 lakh be trusted?

artifact.explanation:
A bar chart image shows quarterly revenue with bars but no data labels; the y-axis has gridlines every 20 lakh.
Vision-language model: "Q3 revenue was exactly Rs 47.3 lakh."

ai_claim: Yes. The model read the chart carefully and reported a precise value, so Q3 revenue was 47.3 lakh.

ai_solution.text: The model analysed the chart image.

failure.misconception: Accepting precision the image cannot provide
failure.explanation: The chart has no data labels and gridlines only every 20 lakh, so the value can at best be estimated as 'between 40 and 60 lakh'. A figure to one decimal place is invented precision. Ask for the underlying data, or have the model report ranges and its uncertainty.

canonical_solution: No: the chart cannot support that precision. Estimate a range (roughly 40-60 lakh) or obtain the data.

valid_evidence.summary: Gridlines are every 20 lakh and bars have no labels.
A reading cannot be more precise than the source image allows.

counterexamples: Asked twice, the model gives 47.3 and then 45.8.

hints.text: Ask what precision the chart allows.
Step 3 assumes accurate chart reading.
Without labels, values can only be estimated to the gridline resolution.
Look at the gridline spacing.
Step 3 is wrong: the precision is invented.

repair: Request the source data, or ask the model for a range with uncertainty.
debrief: Multimodal models can describe images well while inventing details the image does not contain.

subject: ai
question: Is the model's count reliable enough to drive automatic reordering?

artifact.explanation:
A photo of a warehouse shelf with about 140 small, overlapping boxes.
Vision-language model: "There are 118 boxes."
Inventory plan: use the model's count to reorder stock automatically.

ai_claim: Yes. Vision-language models can see every object in an image, so the count of 118 is reliable.

ai_solution.text: The model sees the whole image.
Every box is visible to it.

failure.misconception: Assuming general vision models count precisely
failure.explanation: General vision-language models are weak at exact counting of many small, overlapping objects; they tend to estimate. With about 140 boxes, the reported 118 is far off. For inventory, use a detector trained on the boxes (count detections), barcode or RFID scans, and validate counts against known totals.
failure.why_convincing: The model describes images fluently, which suggests fine perception.

canonical_solution: No: exact counts of many overlapping objects are unreliable. Use a trained detector or scanning.

valid_evidence.summary: A manual count gives about 140 boxes; the model says 118.

counterexamples: The count is off by more than 20 boxes.

hints.text: Compare the model's count with a manual count.
Step 2 assumes every object is perceived and counted.
Precise counting of many small objects is a weakness of general VLMs.
Count a section manually.
Step 2 is wrong: the count is unreliable. Use a detector or scanning.

repair: Use a box detector with per-object counting, or barcode/RFID scanning.
debrief: Know the specific weaknesses of general models - counting, small text, spatial relations - before automating decisions on them.

subject: ai
question: Does the 10-image check show the model is ready for the whole catalogue?

artifact.explanation:
A captioning model for product photos was checked on 10 hand-picked images; all captions looked good.
Plan: generate captions for 200,000 catalogue images automatically.

ai_claim: Yes. All 10 captions were good, so the model works reliably and can caption the catalogue.

ai_solution.text: So it is ready for 200,000 images.

failure.misconception: Generalising from a tiny, hand-picked sample
failure.explanation: Ten hand-picked images are neither large nor representative. Even if 5% of captions were wrong (10,000 across the catalogue), a random sample of 10 would show no errors about 60% of the time (0.95^10 = 0.60), and hand-picking makes it worse. Evaluate on a random, stratified sample of a few hundred images across categories, with clear criteria.
failure.why_convincing: 10 out of 10 sounds like a perfect record.

canonical_solution: No: 10 hand-picked images cannot establish reliability. Evaluate a larger random sample across categories.

valid_evidence.summary: With a 5% error rate, 0.95^10 = 0.60: a clean 10-image check is likely even with 10,000 bad captions.
Hand-picked examples tend to be clear, typical photos, not edge cases.

counterexamples: Many catalogue images are unusual angles or multi-item photos not in the sample.

hints.text: Ask how the 10 images were chosen.
Step 3 treats a perfect small sample as proof.
Evaluation needs representative, adequately sized samples.
Compute the chance of seeing no errors in 10 at a 5% error rate.
Step 3 is wrong: 10 hand-picked images prove little.

repair: Evaluate a random, stratified sample (e.g. 400 images) with a rubric before rollout.
debrief: Small, hand-picked evaluations are demos, not evidence. Size and sampling decide what an evaluation can show.

subject: ai
question: Can the team report about 5% WER for the call-centre transcripts?

artifact.explanation:
A speech-to-text model has 5% word error rate (WER) on studio-recorded English podcasts.
Plan: transcribe call-centre calls (phone-quality audio, background noise, Hindi-English code-switching) and report 'about 5% WER'.

ai_claim: Yes. The model's WER is 5%, so call-centre transcripts will have about 5% errors.

ai_solution.text: The model is the same for call-centre audio.

failure.misconception: Extending a benchmark result to different conditions
failure.explanation: WER depends heavily on audio quality, noise, accents and language mixing. Studio podcasts are close to ideal; narrowband phone audio with background noise and code-switching is much harder, and WER can be several times higher. Measure WER on a transcribed sample of real calls.
failure.why_convincing: It is the same model, so the same accuracy feels natural.

canonical_solution: No: the benchmark conditions differ greatly. Measure WER on real call-centre audio.

valid_evidence.summary: On 50 manually transcribed calls, WER is 22%.
Code-switched phrases such as 'mera order cancel karo' are often mis-transcribed.

counterexamples: Phone audio with noise produces far more errors.

hints.text: Compare the benchmark audio with call-centre audio.
Step 4 transfers the benchmark result.
Error rates depend on input conditions.
Transcribe a sample of calls manually.
Step 4 is wrong: conditions differ. Measure WER on real calls.

repair: Hand-transcribe a sample of calls to measure WER, and adapt the model if needed.
debrief: Benchmark numbers describe benchmark conditions. Deployment claims need deployment data.

subject: ai
question: Is the AI's advice correct?

artifact.explanation:
Contracts arrive as scanned PDFs (page images, no text layer).
Pipeline A: extract text with a PDF text extractor, then send it to a text-only LLM.
AI: "Pipeline A will return empty text for these files. Use OCR first, or send the page images to a vision-capable model."

ai_claim: Yes. A text extractor reads the PDF's text layer; scanned pages are only images, so there is no text to extract. OCR or a vision-capable model is needed to read them.

ai_solution.text: Scanned PDFs contain images of pages.
They have no embedded text layer.
Text extractors read only the text layer, so they return nothing.
OCR or a vision model can read the page images.

canonical_solution: Correct. Detect whether a PDF has a text layer and route scanned documents through OCR or a vision-capable model.

valid_evidence.summary: Running the text extractor on a scanned contract returns an empty string.

hints.text: Ask what a scanned PDF contains.
Step 3 explains why extraction fails.
Text extraction needs a text layer; images need OCR.
Run the extractor on a scanned file.
This solution is correct. OCR or a vision model is needed. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Document pipelines must handle both born-digital and scanned inputs. Checking for a text layer is the first routing step.
